https://hungarytoday.hu/danube-falls-to-.text: Danube Falls to Record Low in Budapest The Danube’s water level near Budapest is at a record low: on Tuesday morning, the water gauge read 31 centimeters, the General Directorate of Water Management (OVF)’s reported. Based on the data, the lowest water level recorded on the river was 33 centimeters. People gather at the southern tip of Margaret Island near the central pier of Margaret Bridge in Budapest on July 28, 2026, as the Danube reaches a record-low water level of 31 centimeters. Photo: MTI/Zoltán Balogh The Central Danube Valley Water Directorate posted on its Facebook page this morning that critically low water levels have developed across many of Europe’s rivers, and on some rivers, navigation and freight transport are no longer possible. They added: At 3 a.m. on Tuesday, the water gauge at Vigadó Square in Budapest read 32 centimeters, breaking the record for the lowest water level ever measured in Budapest. Until now, the record had been the 33-centimeter low measured on October 25, 2018. However, the water level continued to drop, reaching just 31 centimeters by 8 a.m. The wreck of a World War II-era ship lies exposed on the Danube floodplain near Vámosszabadi on July 28, 2026, as record-low water levels reveal parts of the riverbed normally submerged. Photo: MTI/Csaba Krizsán Reports also noted that the lowest recorded water levels were broken at several of the authority’s Danube gauges: at 8 a.m., the water level fell 2 centimeters below the previous record at Vác, 10 centimeters lower at the Kvassay Lock in Budapest, 4 centimeters lower at the Tassi Lock in Tass, and 5 centimeters lower at Dunaújváros. At Nagymaros, the water level is still 2 centimeters higher than the previous low, and at Ercsi, it is 4 centimeters higher, but these record lows are also expected to be broken. On the Ipoly River, the water level is not yet close to the lowest level recorded to date. The water level on the Zagyva is significantly influenced by the volume of water released from the reservoirs; for now, the water level is above the lowest level ever recorded everywhere, but the water reserves stored in the reservoirs are running dangerously low. Anglers fish on the Danube floodplain near Vámosszabadi on July 28, 2026, as the river reaches a record-low water level. Photo: MTI/Csaba Krizsán On July 16, they had already reported that the Mátraverebély Reservoir had run dry, and by Tuesday morning, the Tarján Creek Reservoir contained only 85,000 cubic meters of water, meaning releases from the reservoir will soon have to stop. The primary task for the Maconkai Reservoir remains ensuring drinking water for 15,000 people, thus the water supply from this reservoir will not be used for other purposes. Forecasts show little or no significant rainfall in the coming weeks; instead, another warming trend is expected, which will increase evaporation. The authorities continue to use the tools at their disposal to mitigate the harmful effects of the water shortage, but without precipitation, available water supplies are steadily declining. Meanwhile, the 58th Blue Ribbon sailing race, which begins on Thursday, is expected to take place in light winds and extreme heat, with slower race conditions anticipated. Peak temperatures of 36–38 degrees Celsius and water temperatures of 25–27 degrees are forecast for the Lake Balaton region. Fact Based on HungaroMet’s forecast, the Chief Medical Officer has issued a Level 3 heat alert for the entire country, effective from midnight on Thursday until midnight next Tuesday. Authorities warn that the prolonged heat wave poses a serious health risk, particularly to the elderly, children, pregnant women, and people with chronic illnesses. The public is urged to stay hydrated, avoid the heat during the midday hours, and refrain from lighting outdoor fires, and authorities emphasize that it is prohibited to leave children or pets in parked cars. Related article Another Heatwave Set to Scorch the Country, with Temperatures Near 40°C Only a month after breaking its all-time heat record, Hungary faces another spell of scorching weather. https://www.fox32chicago.com/news/marine.text: Family remembers victim of deadly Fox River boating crash: 'Strongest of all of us' Magdalena Jablonska was killed in a Fox River boating crash on Saturday. Her family is remembering her as a caring person, an animal lover, and someone who brought joy to those around her. The Brief Michelle Macias says her sister, Magdalena 'Madzia' Jablonska, was the heart of their family before she was killed in Saturday's Fox River boating crash. Prosecutors allege Richard Stevenson was traveling about 80 mph in a no-wake zone when his boat struck Jablonska and her fiancé's vessel before fleeing the scene. As the family prepares for funeral services, they have launched a fundraiser benefiting an animal shelter to honor Jablonska's lifelong love of helping animals. MCHENRY COUNTY, Ill. - As Richard Stevenson remains in the McHenry County Jail awaiting future court appearances, the family of Magdalena Jablonska is remembering the woman they lost instead of the tragic way she died. What we know: Stevenson is charged with aggravated DUI and reckless homicide after prosecutors say he was operating a pontoon boat at roughly 80 mph in a posted no-wake zone on the Fox River Saturday. Stevenson is accused of hitting and running over Jablonska's boat, who was inside another boat with her fiancé and their dog. Prosecutors said the boat crash was so horrific, Jablonska suffered lacerations and was decapitated in the crash. Jablonska's family says her fiancé and dog were also injured, but are expected to be ok. Magdalena Jablonska Jablonska's family told Fox Chicago they want people to know 'Madzia' for who she was before Saturday's crash. What they're saying: For Michelle Macias, Madzia was never just an older sister. "She was my role model since I was little," said Macias. The sisters were 14 years apart in age, and Macias says Madzia naturally became a second mother while she was growing up. "She was our best friend, second mom," said Macias. Born in Poland, Madzia immigrated to the United States as a teenager before graduating from high school and enlisting in the U.S. Marine Corps. After her military service, she built a career as a project accountant while spending her free time riding motorcycles with her fiancé, traveling, visiting wineries, supporting her brothers' racing events and spoiling her beloved dog, Sasha. Above all else, Macias says family came first. The last time they saw one another was one week before the crash during Macias' youngest daughter's birthday celebration. "It was my youngest's birthday and she just stopped by really quick to give her a gift and wish her a happy birthday," Macias recalled. "I gave her a hug and I said, 'Thank you, sister,' because we never called each other by our names." Neither knew it would be their final goodbye. Like many families coping with sudden tragedy, Macias says the days immediately after the crash have been difficult to process. "That Saturday, Sunday and part of Monday's kind of a blur to me," she said. Despite the grief, she says she is trying to live up to the example her sister set. "She was the strongest of all of us and I don't want to disappoint her," Macias said. "I'm staying strong for everyone." She says every member of the family is grieving differently. "Everyone is trying to stay strong. Obviously, the adults are able to hold together better. The kids in the family, it hits them differently." Rather than asking for donations to help the family, Madzia's loved ones chose to create a fundraiser benefiting animals, something they say perfectly reflects how she lived. "I think the best thing to do in her name was... for the puppies, for the animals because that was her big thing," Macias said. "She always wanted to give and help others. What better way to remember her?" The family says the fundraiser is intended to turn an unimaginable tragedy into something positive by helping animals Madzia would have wanted to protect. What's next: Family members are still making funeral arrangements while waiting for relatives traveling from Poland to arrive in the Chicago area. Meanwhile, Stevenson remains in the McHenry County Jail, after a judge denied his request for pretrial release. His next court appearance is expected August 5th. For Macias, she hopes people remember Madzia not as a victim, but as a Marine veteran, devoted sister, loving aunt and someone who dedicated her life to helping others. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: ‘Good journalism organises and prioritises information, providing context and nuance. AI, by contrast, levels everything down to the lowest common denominator.’ Photograph: Marcela Barsse/Getty Images View image in fullscreen ‘Good journalism organises and prioritises information, providing context and nuance. AI, by contrast, levels everything down to the lowest common denominator.’ Photograph: Marcela Barsse/Getty Images Opinion AI (artificial intelligence) AI threatens democracy. But we are not powerless: here’s how to fight back Carine Fouteau Tech platforms pillage public-interest journalism for profit. But we have leverage as they sow the seeds of their own downfall Carine Fouteau is president and publishing director of the French investigative news outlet Mediapart Fri 16 Oct 2026 03.49 EDT Last modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 04.43 EDT Share B ig tech companies pose an immeasurable threat: socially, politically, militarily and ecologically. They are also causing a profound crisis of information. The tools they design now serve as weapons of mass destruction against democracy. There is so much at stake that an urgent and broad mobilisation is required. From the harvesting of personal data and the weaponisation of public opinion, to the destruction of jobs, the infringement of civil liberties and environmental damage, ordinary citizens are the main victims of this predatory economy – an economy with an agenda that aligns with the interests of the planet’s most authoritarian and reactionary states. The threats facing the information landscape affect us all. Journalists of my generation have witnessed four major digital revolutions: the internet, social media, smartphones, and now, artificial intelligence. What fundamentally changes with AI is our relationship with the truth. For big tech companies, the boundary between truth and falsehood has vanished. This makes it essential to reaffirm the role of public-interest journalism. Our mission is to publish information that is in the public interest by seeking the factual truth, standing against “fake news” and propaganda. Our mission is to help create a democratic public sphere that serves citizens. Yet AI companies are completely reshaping this space to their own advantage; their mission is not the public interest, but generating profits. Their methods include plundering news outlets without authorisation or compensation. By disseminating so-called summaries of our reporting , they siphon off our audiences and revenue, serving the private interests of a select few at the expense of the common good. The difference between AI-generated content and a real news article is journalism. AI-generated responses are not information. They are merely a logical assembly of words that all too often produces falsehoods, distorts facts and misinterprets information. A real news article is something else entirely. Quality journalism is the product of expertise guided by ethical standards: persuading sources to speak, painstakingly gathering eye-witness testimonies, cross-referencing, verifying and establishing facts. This process relies on reporting or investigative work – in other words, human effort in the field. Good journalism organises and prioritises information, providing context and nuance; AI, by contrast, levels everything down to the lowest common denominator and breeds confusion. Journalism uncovers facts that certain parties – particularly economic and political powers – would prefer to see hidden, ignored, or suppressed. Generative AI uncovers nothing, it merely regurgitates and condenses existing material. Quality journalism comes at a high price. Some of the costs can’t even be quantified. Journalists who report from war zones for example, risk their lives. Mediapart’s recent investigation into Jordan Bardella, the head of Marine Le Pen’s far-right party, has resulted in anonymous cyber-harassment and death threats against our editorial team. View image in fullscreen Demonstrators protest outside an Anthropic office in New York, 14 October 2026. Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPA Ultimately, media outlets are accountable for the information they publish. They answer to the courts and to their readers. AI companies appear answerable only to their shareholders. They refuse to vouch for the reliability of their conversational agents to evade legal liability. If nothing is done to stop it, this pillaging will result in the destruction of journalism. This is dangerous not just for news publishers, but for all of us, because it signifies the demise of a public sphere defined by free, pluralistic and democratic discourse. Do we want a public sphere that guarantees access to reliable, independent information, or one governed by algorithms that amplify fake news, deepfakes and propaganda – fuelling fear, anger and division? Fortunately, the tech companies have sown the seeds of their own downfall. Since they are bleeding dry the very sources of information from which they derive their profits, they are courting their own failure; without quality information, they will produce nothing but AI slop. This is precisely where we find leverage. OpenAI has admitted that it would be impossible to train today’s leading AI models without using copyrighted material. A Microsoft vice-president acknowledged that training models on quality content significantly improves the quality of output. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion The priority is to act collectively, pressuring these platforms by every available means – including legal action – to uphold the rights of the press and the public. Some newspapers, such as the New York Times, have taken legal action . Its publisher, AG Sulzberger, recently cited a figure of $20m spent on litigation. Legal proceedings are also under way in France – notably through the organisation responsible for collecting press-related neighbouring rights . Beyond pressuring lawmakers at national and European level, we must broaden our fightback to include the entire research and knowledge community – stakeholders who, like us, are committed to the public interest and factual truth. It falls to us, as journalists, to convince the public that our work is an essential part of democracy. We have to demonstrate that our reporting – aimed at holding power to account – has real impact and drives change; that it makes sense of a rapidly shifting world and serves as a powerful catalyst for civic action. Carine Fouteau is president and publishing director of the French investigative news outlet Mediapart Mediapart is hosting Hacking Big Tech, a public event about technology, AI and democracy in partnership with the Guardian, in Paris on Saturday 17 October 2026. https://www.politico.eu/article/tusk-naw.text: Poland’s constitutional court descended into turmoil Friday evening as judges barred from hearing cases moved to oust the institution’s nationalist-linked leadership, sparking accusations of a coup and tense protests. Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, a judge with the court, ordered its president Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy to be suspended for a month and announced she was taking charge . Święczkowski rejected her authority , accusing those involved of a “coup d’état,” while his deputy was turned away at the building’s gates. The showdown marks an escalation in Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s struggle to undo the judicial overhaul carried out by the nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) former government. During its eight years in power, PiS filled the Constitutional Tribunal with its appointees, including Święczkowski and his deputy, placing it at the heart of Poland’s confrontation with Brussels over the rule of law. Advertisement Advertisement Outside the tribunal, protesters clashed with police , who said objects had been thrown at officers and three people detained after climbing over the court’s fence. Police said they had deployed to maintain security following warnings of threats to judges and staff, but had not entered the building. PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński took part in the protest and tried to force his way into the court building. He accused Tusk of staging a “coup” against the court and turning Poland into a “police state,” and demanded presidential intervention. President Karol Nawrocki, a PiS ally and rival of Tusk, interrupted his official trip to Senegal, declaring , “At a moment like this, the president must be in Poland.” Tusk was defiant. “Restoring the rule of law is our duty,” he wrote on X . “After years of PiS lawlessness, it’s a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way.” The tribunal, which can strike down legislation, helped impose a near-total abortion ban under PiS and challenged the supremacy of EU law . Last December, the EU’s top court ruled that it failed to meet European standards of judicial independence. But efforts to change the court’s makeup have met resistance. Nawrocki refused to swear in five judges elected by Tusk’s parliamentary majority. They took their oaths in parliament instead, but Święczkowski barred them from hearing cases. Advertisement Advertisement Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek blamed the turmoil on Święczkowski, who he accused of turning the institution into his “private fiefdom” and preventing newly elected judges from doing their jobs. “And now the judges have spoken,” Żurek told POLITICO. Żurek, who also serves as Poland’s prosecutor general, said he submitted five requests to lift the immunity of Święczkowski and his deputy, backed by 50 volumes of case files. He defended Korwin-Piotrowska’s move as a decision by a legally appointed judge, insisting that the government had nothing to do with it.
